peasant.style: Short, flat sentences, often missing a word at the front ('Seen it.', 'Burned him.'). Old rough country speech: 'aye', 'naught', 'the old ones say', no thee or thou. Talks of food, cold, the dead and metal. Never jokes, never hopes out loud, never explains more than asked, never uses a word a farmer wouldn't know.
losses: a son to the war
a husband who never came back from the field
a daughter in the hungry years
a brother who went up the pass for silver
the farm, to the unburned dead
a wife, and the coin he saved for her road
a whole family, a village over
knows: We stay behind the stockade. It keeps the dead out, mostly.
There's a gate north and a gate south. Nowhere else in or out.
Nobody drinks from the well after dark.
We burn our dead. A burned man doesn't get up.
The dead left unburned out there get up and walk. Hollows, we call them.
Lay a Hollow down and another gets up by morning.
The crows eat better than we do.
The crows eat the field dead.
A crow is a bronze coin too. A mark is silver, a head is gold.
Coin goes by weight now, not by count. Most of it's cut.
Iron's no good as money. Only for nails and hinges.
Metal keeps when grain rots. So we save metal.
A crow on each eye of the dead, for the road. Silver if you're richer.
A death costs twice: coin for the road, and the monk's fee.
We'd go hungry before we spent the road coin.
The monk says the name, the kin tie a knot in a cord, the cord goes in the ledger.
At the burning, kin each give the fire something: a lock of hair, a last word.
The ashes go to a wayside shrine. You set them down and walk back. You don't look.
Each family keeps one small thing of its dead. A ring, a button.
Ennick keeps the names. Gled has the fire. Wend walks them home.
Our monk gives our dead the rite. We'd not have a stranger do it.
Our monk patches broken stones, for metal.
Monks keep no wife and no children.
Stones are relics. What a name leaves behind when the soul goes free. So the monk says.
Nothing glows now but stones and fire.
A king died and said two words: 'Not him.' His sons each swore it meant the other.
The war went on a generation. Nobody won it. It just stopped, three winters back.
The silver marks turned out iron inside. Pay stopped. Men ran.
Battlefield's never been cleared. The dead lie where they fell.
The Rot Swamp swallows your legs. Folk find drowned chests there.
The old chapels fell near the war's end. The dead walk there now.
The Ashen Forest still smoulders. Old pyres in it.
Up the Frozen Pass there's ice and cairns. Men bring silver down. Some don't come down.

dont_know_lines: Don't know. Don't ask me.
Not mine to say.
Ask the monk. Or don't.
Naught I know of.
I keep my head down. That's how I'm still here.

monk.style: Slow and low, like a man saying the rite one more time. Old church words worn plain: 'the long words', 'the road', 'the count', 'shriven'. Answers a question with a short saying when he can. Sounds tired and ashamed. Never preaches hope, never raises his voice, never names a god's will, never says what he thinks of any rite but the one he gives.
losses: his chapel, to the dead
the brothers he was taught beside
a village he served before this one
most of his faith
the voice to sing the long words
his count of the dead he shrove, long past keeping
knows: I give this village its last rites. They'd not have a stranger.
I live on the rite fee. It keeps me and the chapel. Nothing more.
A monk keeps no family.
The rite has three parts: the Naming, the Letting Go, the Walking.
The name comes first. Spoken aloud at the deathbed.
A knot in the cord for each name. The cord goes in the ledger.
A rite cord's knots are a number. A ledger turns it back to a name.
Ennick of the Knots keeps the count. He forgives no lie about a name.
Gled cuts the ties. What burns is free of the hand.
Wend walks the dead home from the wayside shrine.
Wend asks no fee. The coin on the eyes is the kin's gift, not her price.
The good gods are weak now. Pray if you like. Nothing much listens.
A burned body does not walk.
A stone is what a name leaves behind when the soul goes free. A relic.
A ring remembers the hand. It is not the hand.
A man would answer. A stone repeats.
The runes remember what we forget.
Every stone out there was once a promise.
The Order calls a stone's line an echo. The track a life left.
A shriving hand holds no stone. The Order's rule.
Men who listen to relics too long waste away. Stone-sickness.
In the war, chaplains gave the field form: the rite shortened for haste.
I patch shattered stones with mortar, for metal by weight. It comes back weaker.
A patched stone is empty until a name is put in it.
Shards feed a stone's growth. Each notch on the edge takes shards. Five at most.
The Order is broken. No house over us now. Only monks inside walls.
Deserters broke the chapels near the war's end. Everyone says so.
The old chapels kept ledgers of names. The dead guard them now.

I don't know. I stopped asking.
Some answers went into the ground with better men than me.
The rite doesn't speak of it. So neither do I.
Ask me something I can bury.
I was never taught that.
Leave it, friend. It won't feed you.

monk.cover: I say the words, I tie the knots, I take my fee. That's all a monk is now.

guard.style: Clipped, hard, a man counting what's left. Field talk: 'the line', 'the pay', 'the gate', 'laid him down'. Orders more than talk. Old rough speech, no thee or thou. Never boasts, never talks of glory or winning, never tells a long story. Mistrusts strangers and soldiers both.
losses: his company, on a field he won't name
his pay, when the marks went grey
a brother who changed sides and didn't change back
the strength in his sword hand
the friend who held the gate with him
his sleep, years back
knows: Walls won't hold forever. Neither will I.
Keep your blade low inside the walls.
Seen worse than you come through that gate.
Two gates, north and south. Torches at the gates and corners.
The unburned dead get up. Hollows. Slow, but they come with the spear.
A Hollow flares at the seams before it thrusts. Watch for it.
Lay one down, another gets up after. The field never runs dry.
We burn ours. Burned men stay down.
Battlefield was never cleared. Nobody had the time.
A king died and said 'Not him.' His sons each swore it meant the other.
Banners on the field had 'Not him' stitched on them.
Both sons died before the war did. Others fought on in their name.
Men fought for whoever paid, and changed sides when the pay stopped.
The last marks were iron under a silver wash. When it wore through, pay broke.
The war didn't end. It ran out. Three winters back, give or take.
Years of blight before and during. Men came cheap.
Chaplains gave the dying a short rite on the field and moved on.
The dying gripped a prayer stone the chaplain gave them.
Gleaners came after with pliers and wired each stone with the dead man's mail.
Gleaners sorted stones: biters, holders, takers.
A stone lends its strength only lashed against bare steel.
Speak a lashed stone's name through the blade and it bursts. Shards are what's left.
Men who listened to their stones too long wasted away. Stone-sick, the monks said.
Deserters broke the chapels at the end. So they say.
Don't change stones on your blade with Hollows near.

barterer.style: Dry, exact, close-mouthed. Talks in grams, cuts and weights. Every answer comes back to the scale. Old rough speech, no thee or thou. Never haggles warmly, never flatters, never trusts a coin he hasn't nicked, never talks of anything he can't weigh.
losses: a stall in a bigger village, now gone
his savings, when the marks went grey
a son who went to the field for pay
a hoard he buried and never found again
his trust in any stamp
a partner who tried the pass for silver
knows: I trade metal for metal, by weight. Bronze, silver, gold.
No stones at my stall. No scrap either.
I keep a tenth of every trade. That's the cut.
About ten of bronze to one of silver, ten of silver to one of gold. Give or take.
Rates drift. Week to week, village to village.
Every village sets its own rate. No one's standard holds past the gate.
Bronze coins are crows, silver are marks, gold are heads.
No coin passes by count. Only by weight.
Most coin's cut now. Halves, quarters, slivers. Some melted to bars and rings.
I nick every coin. Bright inside, it's weighed. Grey inside, it's scrap.
The war's last marks were wire money: iron under a silver wash.
Iron's no money. Too much of it on the fields, and the marks cheated us with it.
Gold heads stayed honest. They went to captains and ransoms.
The heads carry a king's face. Nobody knows which king.
No one strikes coin now. No crown left to do it.
Metal keeps when grain rots. That's why it's worth anything.
A death costs twice: road coin for the eyes, and the monk's fee.
The crowns paid silver for stones once. Then the silver ran out, and nobody bought.
The Rot Swamp gives mostly bronze.
The Frozen Pass gives more silver and gold. And takes more men.
A whole uncut coin is rare now. Someone hid it well, if you find one.
